summary: Defines Session Description Protocol offer/answer procedures for negotiating and establishing a DTLS association, and the criteria for when a new one must be set up. It updates RFC 5763 and RFC 7345 by replacing their SDP-related text. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Before two programs whisper secrets to each other, they must agree on how. This document explains the exact steps for agreeing to use a secret code, and when they should start over with a fresh one.

subtitle: A single SDP attribute, tls-id, says whether two endpoints should reuse their DTLS association or start a new one.

tldr.problem: When ICE is used, it was unclear from an SDP offer or answer whether a new DTLS association was needed, because the ICE ufrag changes both when ICE is negotiated and when ICE restarts.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines general SDP offer/answer procedures for DTLS and a new media-level attribute, tls-id, whose value pair from the offerer and answerer identifies a DTLS association. A new value signals a new association.
tldr.outcome: The procedures are shared by all DTLS usages, replace parts of RFC 5763 and RFC 7345, and can also be applied to TLS connections.

today: RFC 8842 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9725. It updates RFC 5763 and RFC 7345.

sections.title: Common DTLS Procedures for SDP
sections.content:
RFC 5763 defines SDP offer/answer procedures for DTLS-SRTP, and RFC 7345 does the same for UDPTL over DTLS. This document turns the procedures of RFC 5763 into general ones for DTLS. Other specifications that define a specific DTLS usage can reference it, so that the DTLS aspects are the same everywhere. That matters when several usages share one DTLS association (RFC 8843). It updates RFC 5763 and RFC 7345 by replacing their common offer/answer text with a reference to itself.

The motivation is a gap in RFC 5763. It says a new DTLS association MUST be set up when transport parameters change, but with ICE (RFC 8445) that change is poorly defined. The ufrag value changes both when ICE is negotiated and when ICE restarts, and these events do not always need a new association. There was no way to say explicitly in SDP that a new one was required. The new tls-id attribute fills that gap.
sections.eli5: Two people already had rules for starting a secret chat, but no clear way to say "let us start a new chat". This adds one.

sections.title: When a New DTLS Association Is Needed
sections.content:
After a successful offer/answer exchange, a new DTLS association must be established in these cases:

  • the negotiated DTLS setup roles change;
  • one or more fingerprint values are modified, added or removed in an offer or answer;
  • the intent is explicitly signaled by changing the value of the tls-id attribute.

The first two come from RFC 5763, and the third is new. A new association can only come from a successful offer/answer exchange, so an entity that decides it needs one MUST start an exchange. Here a new association means either the first one between two endpoints or one that replaces an earlier association.

If an endpoint changes its local address or port and that requires a new association, it MUST change its local tls-id. The same applies if the transport forbids a DTLS association from spanning several 5-tuples and the 5-tuple changes. DTLS over SCTP is the RFC's example. It also applies when the endpoint changes a local ICE ufrag and the change requires a new association.
sections.eli5: If you swap roles, change your ID card, or say outright "new chat please", you start over. Otherwise you keep the old chat going.

sections.title: The tls-id Attribute
sections.content:
The tls-id attribute is a media-level SDP attribute. The pair of values, one from the offerer and one from the answerer, uniquely identifies the DTLS association or TLS connection. The value is 20 to 255 characters from letters, digits and + / - _, for example a=tls-id:abc3de65cddef001be82.

Each time an endpoint asks for a new association it MUST generate a new local value. The value MUST come from a strong random function and include at least 120 bits of randomness. An unchanged value, with unchanged fingerprints, means the endpoint wants to reuse the existing association.

No default exists. If an offer or answer has no tls-id, which can happen with older implementations, a change to the DTLS setup role, the fingerprint set or the local transport parameters is treated as a request for a new association. A ufrag change alone is not.

The mux category is IDENTICAL, so it applies to all multiplexed media descriptions, but it is associated only with the m= line carrying the BUNDLE tag. For RTP media it applies to the whole media description and MUST NOT be defined per source with ssrc.
sections.eli5: The tag is a long random name for a chat. Each side picks its own, and the two names together identify the chat.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Procedures
sections.content:
Negotiation uses three SDP attributes: setup (from RFC 4145) for the DTLS roles, fingerprint (from RFC 8122) for certificate fingerprints, and tls-id. The holdconn value of setup MUST NOT be used. The certificate seen in the DTLS handshake MUST match a fingerprint from SDP, otherwise the endpoint MUST tear down the media session immediately.

Initial offer. The offerer MUST include setup with value actpass, one or more fingerprints, and a unique tls-id. Because of actpass, it must be ready to receive a DTLS ClientHello before the answer arrives. Data received before the matching fingerprint is known is treated as coming from an unverified source.

Answer. The answerer includes setup and fingerprints. If a new association is needed, it inserts a new unique tls-id. If it does not accept a new association it MUST reject the m= lines. If no new association is needed, it repeats its previous tls-id, roles and fingerprints. If the offer had no tls-id, the answer MUST NOT include one. With setup:active the answerer starts the handshake.

Offerer processing. If the offerer becomes DTLS client, it MUST establish the association. If it becomes server, it waits.

Modifying the session. A later offer wanting a new association carries a new tls-id. One wanting to keep the old association repeats the old tls-id and the same fingerprint set. Either way setup is actpass.

The offerer and answerer each create their own value, and certificates may be reused across associations. So only the combination of both tls-id values identifies an association. An example is SIP forking, where one offerer value is used for associations with each answerer.
sections.eli5: The caller says "I can be either the one who starts the secret chat or the one who waits", plus an ID photo. The other side picks a role and shows its own ID photo. A new chat name means starting fresh.

sections.title: ICE, UDP Ordering and Forking
sections.content:
Over an unordered transport such as UDP, old and new DTLS packets can arrive mixed up. The only way to tell them apart is by 5-tuple, so at least one endpoint MUST allocate a new 3-tuple (transport, source address, source port), meaning an address, port or set of ICE candidates not recently used for another association. With ICE this means a completely new set of candidates. An answerer therefore cannot start a new association unless the offerer initiated an ICE restart. If the answerer wants one, it starts its own ICE restart and a new exchange. An ICE restart does not by default require a new association.

ICE connectivity checks run before the DTLS handshake. Switching between ICE candidates is not a change of local transport parameters from the DTLS point of view.

With SIP forking, separate DTLS associations form between the caller and each callee. The offerer might have to wait for several answers before finding the fingerprint that matches a given handshake, and MUST NOT declare a fingerprint mismatch until it knows no more answers will arrive. For an offerless INVITE, if an association already exists, the generated offer repeats the earlier tls-id and fingerprints, and ICE restart MUST be initiated.
sections.eli5: If old and new messages share one mailbox, you cannot tell them apart. So one side should use a new mailbox for the new chat.

sections.title: TLS and the Updates to Other RFCs
sections.content:
The same procedures can negotiate a TLS connection. In RFC 4145 the connection attribute says whether to open a new TLS connection, and endpoints MUST keep it consistent with tls-id. A connection:new requires a new unique tls-id, while connection:existing requires repeating the old one. Conflicting values mean the message is treated as misformed. Since support by the peer cannot be assumed, connection and tls-id MUST always be used together. The unique values can also help TLS extensions tell connections apart, as in RFC 8844.

The document edits RFC 5763 in Sections 1, 5, 6.6 and 6.7.1, replacing generic offer/answer and ICE text with references to this RFC and swapping a reference to RFC 4572 for RFC 8122. It also replaces Sections 4.1 to 4.5 of RFC 7345 with text pointing to this RFC, and replaces its ICE usage text in Section 5.2.1.
sections.eli5: The same name-tag trick also works for other secret chats, and this document fixes the old rulebooks so they point to the new shared rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The specification does not change the security considerations of DTLS or of the SDP offer/answer mechanism. It only adds the tls-id attribute and clarifies the procedures for negotiating and establishing a DTLS association. It also does not change the actual TLS connection setup. The RFC states that tls-id alone cannot be used to correlate an offer/answer exchange with a TLS connection setup, so no new considerations arise in that area.
sections.eli5: This only gives chats name tags and clearer steps. It does not change how the secret handshake itself works.
